title: Boiling point elevation with a partially dissociated solute: finding the mole percent dissociated
summary: One screen, two dials. Break up the dissolved compound B into 2C + 2D and watch the particle count and the boiling point rise together until the thermometer reads the 408 K the question quotes - and find out along the way why the molar mass of the solvent is never given.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Elevation of boiling point with a partially dissociated solute
subtopics: Ebullioscopic constant from enthalpy of vaporisation
van't Hoff factor from dissociation stoichiometry
Cancellation of an unknown molar mass
concepts: Kb is not a table value here - it follows from the solvent's boiling point and enthalpy of vaporisation
Quoting the enthalpy of vaporisation as 10R makes the gas constant cancel out of Kb entirely
Kb is proportional to the solvent's molar mass and the molality is inversely proportional to it, so their product is independent of the solvent
A colligative property counts particles, so B giving 2C + 2D contributes four particles for every one that dissociates
i = 1 + 3(alpha) for B into 2C + 2D, bounded by 1 and 4
The rise in boiling point is measured from the pure solvent, not the boiling point itself
formulas: Kb = R (Tb0)^2 M_S / dHvap, with M_S in kg per mol
Kb = 16 M_S when Tb0 = 400 K and dHvap = 10R (M_S in g per mol)
m = mass of solute / (molar mass x mass of solvent in kg)
m = 0.25 / M_S for 0.25 % m/m with M_B = 10 M_S
Kb x m = 4.000 K, independent of the solvent

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: Kb from the thermodynamic definition, the molality from the mass percent, i from the measured rise and alpha from the dissociation stoichiometry

The cancellation of the solvent's molar mass checked symbolically with M_S carried as a free symbol - Kb x m reduces to the constant 4 K, so the result holds for every solvent and not merely for the values tried
Back-substitution with M_S = 12, 20, 33.3, 58.5 and 180 g/mol: alpha = 1/3 returns dTb = 8.000000 K and a boiling point of exactly 408 K in every case

Limiting cases: i = 1 + 3 alpha gives i = 1 at alpha = 0 and i = 4 at alpha = 1, bracketing boiling points of 404 K and 416 K, so the measured 408 K is consistent with partial dissociation as the question states
Units confirmed by dimensional analysis: K kg/mol times mol/kg leaves kelvin, and i is dimensionless

The distractors reproduced deliberately: i = 1 + alpha gives 100 %, which the word 'partially' rules out; ignoring dissociation gives 404 K; using Tb in place of dTb gives i = 102, above the ceiling of 4; ignoring the factor of ten in M_B gives a rise of 80 K. None is 33.33

The alternative reading of '0.25 % (mass/mass)' quantified rather than assumed: taking 0.25 g of B in 100 g of solution gives Kb x m = 4.0100 K, i = 1.99500 and 33.17 %. The paper's numbers are chosen so the conventional reading lands on i = 2 exactly and a clean 33.33, which is the intended answer

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which follows the same route (Kb = 16 M_S, Kb x m = 4, i = 2, i = 1 + 3 alpha) and reports the same 33.33. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing

interactivity: The entire experiment is one screen - apparatus, gauges, equation chain, chart and both controls are visible together with no scrolling inside the run
Two controls only, and both are quantities the question actually turns on: the mole percent of B that has dissociated, and the molar mass of the solvent

Twelve drawn units of B sit in the flask and visibly come apart into two C and two D as the dissociation dial turns - the unit at the fractional boundary is caught mid-split, so the transformation is always on screen rather than a before-and-after swap
The particle count in the bay caption rises from 12 to 24 as the dial reaches the answer, which is the van't Hoff factor made countable
A digital thermometer with a probe in the liquid, a vertical scale marked at 400 K for the pure solvent and 408 K for the measurement, and a bar that has to be brought up to the second mark
Seven live gauges - particle count, i, Kb, molality, Kb x m, the rise and the boiling point - with change deltas flashing on every one that moves

A live equation chain that rebuilds Kb from the solvent's own data, converts 0.25 % into a molality, shows the product Kb x m and finishes at the boiling point, with the term that just changed highlighted

The second dial demonstrates the hidden elegance of the question: changing the solvent's molar mass multiplies Kb and divides the molality by the same factor, so Kb x m stays at 4.000 K and the thermometer does not move at all
Every solvent tried is logged in a small table of M_S, Kb, m and Kb x m, and the notebook says in words what the table shows once three have been tried
A chart of boiling point against mole percent dissociated with the measured 408 K line dashed across it and a marker where the dial currently sits
A status line that reports the gap to 408 K in kelvin and which way to move, and says when the dial is close, without ever naming the answer
The meter snaps to the exact reading when the thermometer matches 408.00 K, and the flask then shows 4 of the 12 units broken up - 8 whole B plus 16 fragments
A log of readings the student chooses to keep, with matches marked
A lab notebook that writes itself only when something has actually been demonstrated

Four cards on the wrong answers this question really produces: 100 % from i = 1 + alpha, 404 K from ignoring dissociation, i = 102 from using Tb instead of the rise, and hunting for a molar mass that is not in the paper
A record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity and ends at the mole percent
Answer, record and step-by-step derivation gated until the thermometer matches, with a reveal-anyway escape
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log
